It's January 2035, in the new café “Bei Ingrid”. An old gentleman walks in, wearing a tram driver's cap: Horst “Hotte” Kaminski, almost 90, Ludwig's colleague from the depot back in the seventies. He speaks pure Berlin dialect. Andrei is at the till.
Mornin'! Say, young man, is this Ludwig's granddaughter's café?
Sorry… Pardon? I didn't quite understand.
The café! Ludwig Brandt's! The tram driver's! I've been lookin' for him for a week, right?
Ah, yes! It's his granddaughter Lena's café. Ludwig is sitting at the back there, by the window.
Well then, give me a coffee and two rolls. With butter. And none of that modern stuff with oat milk, right?
One coffee and two rolls with butter. Coming right up.
Brötchen! You hear that? He says Brötchen! In Berlin it's Schrippe, little fella. Where are you from?
Romania! Well, that's great. Then now you're learnin' real German. Berlin German. The other kind is just for offices.
Hotte? Horst Kaminski? You old rascal! I thought you'd died long ago!
Me? No, Ludwig. I'm too tough to die. And you? Still a posh type who talks proper High German whenever he hears a woman?
I learned that from my wife. She was a teacher. But for you, Hotte, I'll talk like in the old days at the depot.

You hear these forms everywhere, including in the Hören B2 exam. You understand them, but in writing (especially formal writing) you use the full form.

Typical Berlin words: die Schrippe (bread roll), die Stulle (slice of bread with something on it), der Späti (shop open late), die Molle (beer), der Kiez (neighbourhood). And the “Berliner Schnauze”: the Berliners' direct, ironic, sometimes abrupt but warm manner.

4. What do you do as a foreign speaker?

You understand the dialect, but you speak standard German. If you imitate Berlin dialect without mastering it, it can sound odd or even mocking. Simple, safe exceptions: “Schrippe” in Berlin bakeries, “Kiez” for neighbourhood, “’n Kaffee, bitte” in speech.
If you don't understand someone: “Entschuldigung, können Sie das noch einmal langsam sagen?” Older Berliners are usually happy to explain.

Horst Kaminski, whom everyone had called just Hotte for seventy years, was born in February 1945 in a cellar in Friedrichshain while the bombs were falling overhead. He always said that was why he was so loud: even as a baby he'd had to shout louder than the sirens. He had joined the BVB at seventeen as a conductor, then became a tram driver, then spent thirty years as an instructor at the Lichtenberg depot, and in that time, as he claimed, he had taught some five hundred young people to drive a tram, among them a certain Kurt Wolff and, for a few weeks in the winter of 1968, a serious young locksmith from Pankow called Ludwig Brandt.

He had found Ludwig through the article in the Berliner Zeitung, the one about the café. His great-granddaughter had read it to him, because his eyes weren't up to it any more. When she got to the sentence “The first customer was Ludwig Brandt, 86, a former tram driver”, Hotte interrupted her. “Brandt? Ludwig Brandt? The beanpole from Pankow who never laughed? He's still alive?” And then he took his old tram driver's cap out of the wardrobe, got his great-granddaughter to show him the way on the phone, and rode the M4 and the M10 right across Berlin to see for himself.

Lena recognised him the moment he walked in, even though she had never seen him. She knew him from Ludwig's stories. “Hotte, the loudest man at the depot,” Ludwig always said. “The only one who hit a cow with a tram and still got promoted.” Hotte was short and plump, with a white moustache and a voice that filled the whole café even though he wasn't shouting. He wore a shabby leather jacket over a shirt he had apparently ironed specially, and on his tram driver's cap there was still an old BVB sticker from the seventies. Customers turned round when he spoke. He didn't notice, or didn't care.

The two old men sat all morning at the window table of the new café, looking out onto Ingrid-Brandt-Platz and the step-free stop. Andrei brought them coffee, then another, then rolls, then cake, and understood about half of what they were saying. Not because of the words, but because Ludwig suddenly spoke differently. Andrei had known Ludwig for six years. He had never heard him talk like that. No “ich”, only “ick”. No “das”, only “det”. No “gut”, only “jut”. And he laughed, as loudly and as often as Andrei had never heard him laugh.

Remember, Ludwig, the first time you drove? Line 46, the Pankow terminus. You were shaking so much I thought you'd fall off the seat. And then you missed the stop. Fifty metres! And the whole tram had to walk back!
It wasn't my fault. The brakes on that old Gotha were done for, you know that perfectly well. And Mr Pohl didn't speak to me for a week.
Pohl! Old Pohl! He didn't speak to me for a week either. In 1963. Because I hit a cow. In Weißensee. With the tram! A cow! Nobody believed me.

Andrei stood behind the till trying not to laugh, and laughed anyway, and Hotte looked at him and shouted: “See, the little fella's laughing! He's already catching on!” Then he went on to tell how the cow belonged to a farmer from Malchow who wanted to drive it across the tracks, and how Hotte had braked at the last moment, so the cow only got a little nudge, sat down indignantly on the tracks and refused to get up for half an hour. “Half the line stood still,” Hotte shouted. “Because of a cow! And in the report I wrote: delay as a result of an animal obstruction.” Ludwig laughed so hard he started coughing. “As a result of an animal obstruction,” he repeated. “Nominal style. Ingrid would have loved it.”

Elif came to the café after school, as she did every day, to get her cocoa, and sat down at the next table with her homework. After ten minutes she had stopped doing her homework and was just listening, wide-eyed. Elif had been born in Berlin, in Prenzlauer Berg, and she understood Berlin dialect, the way all the children at her school understood a bit of it, but she had never heard anyone talk like Hotte. “Mr Brandt,” she finally whispered when Hotte went to the toilet, “why are you suddenly talking like that? Normally you talk like on TV.”

Ludwig laughed. “Because that's how I talked when I was young,” he said, back in High German. “Everyone at the depot talked like that. Then I met… met Ingrid, and she was a teacher and said she wouldn't marry a man who said ‘ick’. It was a joke, of course. But I learned anyway. For her. For fifty years I spoke High German. And now Hotte turns up and after five minutes it's all back, as if it had never gone away.” He looked out of the window at the blue sign with Ingrid's name. “I think she'd have laughed,” he said quietly. “Secretly she always liked my ‘ick’.”

Hotte came back from the toilet and had apparently heard the last sentence. He sat down, breathing heavily, and said nothing for a while. Then, more quietly than before, almost in High German, he talked about his wife, Erna. She had died eleven years ago. She had been a shop assistant at the cooperative store in Lichtenberg and stood at the window every morning at six when he went past her house on the first tram, and he rang the bell twice so she'd know it was him. Forty-two years. “I still ring,” Hotte said. “When I go past our old house on the M4. Only in my head. But I ring.” Ludwig looked at him and said nothing. And Elif, at the next table, didn't write anything in her exercise book this time. She had understood every word.

In the afternoon Leo dropped by, in his BVG uniform, straight from his shift, and when Hotte saw the old BVB badge on his jacket, he suddenly fell silent. He carefully took Leo's jacket between his thumb and forefinger and looked at the badge for a long time. “I had one too,” he said. “Got it in 1962. From Pohl. Lost it in 1990, when they redid the depot.” He looked at Leo, then at Ludwig. “Your grandson?” he asked. Ludwig nodded. “Second year of his apprenticeship. He already drives on his own, under supervision.” Hotte said nothing for a while. Then he clapped Leo on the shoulder, so hard that Leo nearly fell off his chair. “Well then,” he said. “Then watch out, little fella. And don't stop fifty metres too late. We've had that already.”

Leo laughed and sat down next to the two old men. Without knowing what he was setting off, he told them he had promised his grandfather to ring the bell twice when, after his apprenticeship, he drove past Ingrid-Brandt-Platz in his own tram. So his grandfather would know it was him. Hotte went completely silent. He looked at Ludwig, and Ludwig looked at him, and Leo didn't understand why both of them had suddenly become so serious. Then Hotte said, in a voice that for the first time that day didn't sound like Berlin at all: “Twice. Yes. That's right. Twice means: it's me. I'm thinking of you. That's what we all did back then, at the depot. Everyone had someone they rang twice for.” Leo swallowed hard. He had thought he'd come up with it himself.

When Hotte left in the evening, Ludwig and Leo walked him to the stop. It was dark and cold, and the little chestnut tree by the platform had no leaves, but a thin layer of hoarfrost on its branches that glittered in the light of the street lamps. The M1 came, a new step-free tram. Hotte got on, slowly, and turned round once more in the open door. “Ludwig,” he said. “You're the only one left. Of all of us. From the old depot.” He said it in Berlin dialect, but quietly, without laughing. Ludwig nodded. “Come again, Hotte,” he said. “Every Thursday. The coffee's on me.”
Before that, Lena had put some rolls in a bag for him for the journey home, and Hotte had thanked her three times, louder each time.

That evening at home, in Ingrid's armchair, Ludwig looked for a long time at the photo on the shelf: Ingrid at forty, in her classroom, with a book in her hand and that laugh. “Well, Ingrid,” he said quietly, and then, after a pause, with a little smile: “I found an old friend again today. You'd have liked him.” He was almost sure that in the photo she was laughing a little more broadly than usual.

Hotte came again. Every Thursday at ten, on the M4 and the M10, in his old tram driver's cap. He always ordered the same thing: a coffee and two rolls, with butter, no oat milk. In those weeks Andrei learned more Berlin dialect than in the six years before. He learned that “Ick gloob, ick spinne” means you can't believe something, that “Det is ja ’n Ding” expresses amazement, and that when Hotte called someone “Na, du olle Pflaume”, he meant it as the highest compliment. And Elif did her homework every Thursday at the next table, or pretended to, and wrote down in a little notebook all the words she didn't know. After three months the notebook was full. She called it “Hotte's Dictionary” and gave it to him at Easter, belatedly, for his ninetieth birthday.

Reading text: about the Berlin dialect
Read the text about the Berlin dialect. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
Berlin German isn't actually a dialect but an urban dialect that developed from many influences.
A typical feature is “j” instead of “g”: people say “jut” instead of “gut” and “jestern” instead of “gestern”.
Many words come from French, because many Huguenots came to Berlin in the 17th century. “Bulette”, for example, comes from “boulette”.
Today it's mainly older Berliners who speak real Berlin German. Young people mix it with expressions from many languages.
The famous “Berliner Schnauze” is direct, sometimes cheeky, but usually meant from the heart.
